title: Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR): The Masterclass Guide
summary: PVR remains the leading cause of failure in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment repair, characterized by the formation of fibrotic contractile membranes. This infographic provides a comprehensive overview of its pathogenesis, grading, and surgical management strategies.

sections.title: Definition & Pathogenesis
sections.content: PVR is a complex process of wound healing following retinal detachment (RD). It involves the migration and proliferation of RPE cells, glial cells, and fibroblasts, forming epiretinal, subretinal, and periretinal membranes. These membranes exert tractional forces, preventing retinal reattachment.

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending PVR
content: Fixed retinal folds resistant to fluid-air exchange

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with wide-field visualization.
Step 2: Core vitrectomy followed by membrane peeling (Il-M, TPA, or forceps).
Step 3: Relaxing retinectomy (circumferential or radial) to release traction.
Step 4: Fluid-air exchange and internal tamponade (Silicone Oil or C3F8).
Step 5: Post-operative positioning (face-down) for tamponade optimization.

content.explanation: P: Peripheral Relaxing Retinectomy; E: Excision of membranes; E: Endotamponade (Silicon Oil); L: Laser photocoagulation (360°)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Avoid excessive cryotherapy, which releases RPE cells into the vitreous, promoting PVR.
The use of heavy silicone oil (Densiron) may be considered for inferior PVR cases.
Pharmacologic adjuncts like Daunorubicin have shown limited clinical success in preventing PVR recurrence.
Surgical success in PVR (Grade C) is historically < 60% after initial attempt.
